title: Matthew 13:24–30
context: Jesus sets another kingdom parable before the crowds: good seed sown in a field, an enemy’s weeds mixed among the wheat, and a master’s patience until harvest. Premature uprooting is refused; final separation is reserved for the reapers.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Older voices from both traditions on Matthew 13:24–30.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: He proposed another parable - in which he farther explains the case of unfruitful hearers. The kingdom of heaven (as has been observed before) sometimes signifies eternal glory: sometimes the way to it, inward religion; sometimes, as here, the Gospel dispensation: the phrase is likewise used for a person or thing relating to any one of those: so in this place it means, Christ preaching the Gospel, who is like a man sowing good seed - The expression, is like, both here and in several other places, only means, that the thing spoken of may be illustrated by the following similitude.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 13:24–30)

reformed.quote: In order to reap the advantage of this parable, it is necessary to ascertain the object which Christ had in view. Some think that, to guard a mixed multitude against satisfying themselves with an outward profession of the Gospel, he told them, that in his own field bad seed is often mixed with the good, but that a day is coming, when the tares shall be separated from the wheat.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 13:24–30)

verses.text: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field,
verses.arminianNotes:
Another kingdom picture: a man sows good seed in his field. The kingdom’s advance begins with good—seed meant for life, field under the sower’s care.

What comes through is sincere goodness in God’s planting. The parable will introduce evil’s intrusion without blaming the sower’s seed; grace that plants also invites trust in the Master’s eventual justice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ frames the kingdom by a sower’s good seed. The field belongs to the man who plants; goodness is primary, not afterthought.

The Son of Man’s kingdom work starts with His own planting. What follows—weeds, patience, harvest—unfolds under His ownership and purpose.

verses.text: but while people slept, his enemy came and sowed darnel weeds also among the wheat, and went away.
verses.arminianNotes:
While workers sleep, an enemy slips in weeds also among the wheat, and leaves. Evil is parasitic and opportunistic—mixed into what was planted good.

The church lives in a contested field. Grace does not deny the enemy’s malice; hearers are called to wakefulness without panic, trusting the Master more than their own night watch.
verses.reformedNotes:
Enemy action explains the mixture: weeds appear because an adversary sowed them, not because the master’s seed failed.

Providence allows the field’s complexity for a time. Satan’s counterfeit sowing is no illusion; God’s ownership of the field is not cancelled by nocturnal sabotage.

verses.text: But when the blade sprang up and produced grain, then the darnel weeds appeared also.
verses.arminianNotes:
Growth reveals mixture: grain appears, and weeds show themselves too. Early stages can look alike; fruiting time exposes difference.

Arminians urge patient discernment. Grace grows true wheat; imitation also springs up. The church must not confuse every green shoot with harvest-ready righteousness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Appearance follows growth. Weeds become visible as the crop matures—timing that frustrates hasty judgment.

God orders the disclosure of difference. The kingdom’s present form includes mixture until the appointed revealing.

verses.text: The servants of the householder came and said to him, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where did these darnel weeds come from?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Servants are puzzled: good seed was sown—whence the weeds? Honest ministry asks hard questions when evil appears beside the good.

Bring confusion to the Master, not to despair. Grace allows lament and inquiry; the field’s problem does not mean the sower lied about His seed.
verses.reformedNotes:
The servants’ question assumes the master’s goodness and seeks explanation. Theology begins with who sowed, not with panic about weeds.

The master’s character stands unquestioned. Questions about evil in the field are answered by His word, not by rewriting the goodness of His planting.

verses.text: “He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ “The servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and gather them up?’
verses.arminianNotes:
The master names the cause: an enemy. Servants immediately offer zealous weeding—gather them now.

Classical Arminians recognize holy impatience against evil, yet the parable will restrain premature purge. Grace that hates weeds also teaches patience toward a mixed field until God’s timing.
verses.reformedNotes:
The master first diagnoses the problem as the work of an enemy. The servants’ zeal to gather is natural—and about to be corrected.

Identifying Satan’s work does not authorize every human solution. The Master retains the strategy for His field.

verses.text: “But he said, ‘No, lest perhaps while you gather up the darnel weeds, you root up the wheat with them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The master refuses: premature gathering risks uprooting wheat with weeds. Discernment is imperfect; zeal can harm the true crop.

Grace calls for careful love in church discipline and cultural conflict. Separate evil without crushing weak believers; leave final sorting to the Lord of the harvest.
verses.reformedNotes:
“No” protects the wheat. Human reapers now would damage what God intends to keep.

The church’s present authority is true yet limited. Final, perfect separation belongs to the end; interim patience is obedience, not indifference.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm patience that refuses reckless purge. Arminians typically underline responsible, grace-shaped care not to harm true believers while opposing evil; Reformed interpreters emphasize God’s sovereign timing for final separation and the church’s limited mandate before harvest.

verses.text: Let both grow together until the harvest, and in the harvest time I will tell the reapers, “First, gather up the darnel weeds, and bind them in bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”
verses.arminianNotes:
Both grow until harvest; then reapers gather weeds for burning and wheat for the barn. Delay is not denial—judgment and gathering are certain.

Classical Arminians hold urgency and patience together: grace still invites all to become wheat by faith; the coming fire warns that refusal is not forever tolerated. Present mixture does not cancel future accountability.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Master sets the timetable and commands the reapers. Burning and barn are His appointments at harvest.

History moves toward ordered separation under Christ’s word. Wheat is gathered because it is His; weeds face judgment because evil’s end is sure—not because servants forced an early cleanup.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess a future judgment that separates weeds and wheat. Arminians typically highlight sincere present invitation alongside certain judgment; Reformed commentators highlight God’s decree of final separation and the security of the wheat He will gather into His barn.
